610.title: The water you drink, the fire you light
610.hook: have you seen the water you drink, the fire you kindle, who made them (56:68–72)
610.tomorrow: None touch it but the purified
610.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and follow the Prophet's practice of drinking in sips with pauses for breath; these verses of Al-Waqi'ah are recited as a reminder to be grateful for ordinary things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the foremost, and your line was first in good. Who did you greet first? Day six hundred ten.

Turn on a tap and water comes out. Click a lighter and there's a flame. Both happen so many times a day that they don't feel like events at all. Nobody stands at the sink amazed. Surah Al-Waqi'ah, after its great pictures of the Day, turns to the kitchen. It asks four short questions about four ordinary things: the seed of life, the crop, the water, the fire. Each one starts the same way: have you seen? Have you looked, really looked?

Verse sixty-eight. Pickthall: "Have ye observed the water which ye drink?" Then the question behind the question: is it you who bring it down from the rain cloud, or are We the ones who send it? And then a sharp line: if God willed, he could make it bitter, salt; so why don't you give thanks? The same pattern comes a few verses earlier, with the seed from which a person is made, and with the crop: you plant, but who makes it grow? Then the fire. Have you seen the fire you strike? Was it you who made its tree grow, or did God? The Arabs of the time struck fire from green wood. Commentators name two desert trees, markh and 'afar, whose branches were rubbed together to make a flame. Surah Ya-Sin says the same thing: God made fire for you out of the green tree. Green wood, full of sap, and fire comes out of it. Then verse seventy-three gives fire two jobs: a reminder, and a comfort for travelers in the desert, people who needed it to cook, to keep warm, to be seen at night. The questions aren't trick questions. Nobody listening thought they made the rain. The point is the habit of asking. Every glass of water arrives from somewhere: a cloud, a river, a pipe someone laid. The hadith turns drinking into a small, slow act. Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ would breathe three times while drinking, taking it in three sips rather than one gulp. Three pauses, enough time to notice what's in your hand.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN THE WATER YOU DRINK?` · `IT COULD HAVE BEEN BITTER.` · `FIRE FROM THE GREEN TREE.` · `THREE BREATHS WHILE DRINKING.`

segments.voice: The practice: light a candle, drink water. If you can, light a candle or a stove, safely, and pour a glass of water. If not, just picture them. Watch the flame for a few breaths. Then drink the water slowly, in three sips, pausing between each. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah and end with alhamdulillah. With each sip, let today's question rise: who made it? The bell holds the time.
The water you drink. Surah Al-Waqi'ah asks who sends it from the cloud, and why, if it could be bitter, it comes sweet. Today's word.
Your line: who made it? Today, before one glass of water, stop for one breath and ask it. Day six hundred ten.

611.title: None touch it but the purified
611.word: None touch it but the purified
611.hook: a noble Qur'an in a guarded book, touched only by the purified (56:77–79)
611.tomorrow: He is with you wherever you are
611.howItsDone: Most Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it in a high, clean place, and often wrap it in cloth; reciting from memory without wudu is widely permitted, and schools differ on details.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water you drink and the fire you light, and your line was who made it? Did one glass of water get a breath before you drank? Day six hundred eleven.

Walk into many Muslim homes and you'll find the Qur'an on the highest shelf, often wrapped in cloth, nothing stacked on top of it. When someone takes it down, they may pause first, go and wash, and come back. Children learn not to put it on the floor. A guest might be surprised by all the care around one book. Much of that care traces back to three verses near the end of Surah Al-Waqi'ah. And what those verses mean is something Muslim scholars have discussed, with more than one answer, for a very long time.

Verses seventy-seven to seventy-nine. Pickthall: "That (this) is indeed a noble Qur'an In a Book kept hidden Which none toucheth save the purified". Three things are said. The Qur'an is karim, noble, generous. It is in a kitab maknun, a book kept hidden, guarded. And none touches it but the mutahharun, the purified. Here the readings divide. Many classical commentators said the hidden book is the heavenly original, the preserved tablet, and the purified who touch it are the angels. On that reading, the verse describes the Qur'an's source, not a rule for people. Others read the verse as also pointing to the written copy on earth, the mushaf. And most jurists, whichever reading they held for the verse, required ritual purity to touch the mushaf. They leaned as well on a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to 'Amr ibn Hazm in Yemen, preserved in Malik's Muwatta, which said that none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. So the four main Sunni schools, and Shia jurists too, generally hold that you should be in wudu, the washing before prayer, to touch the written Arabic text. A minority of scholars, among them Ibn Hazm of Andalusia, didn't require it. Reciting from memory without wudu is widely allowed. Whatever the ruling, the habit it built is the one in the hook: the book isn't just picked up. It is prepared for. The washing comes first, and the reading after.
screen: `A NOBLE QUR'AN, A BOOK KEPT HIDDEN.` · `THE PURIFIED: ANGELS, SAY MANY.` · `THE LETTER TO 'AMR IBN HAZM.` · `WASH FIRST, THEN READ.`

segments.voice: The practice: make wudu before reading. If you're Muslim, you might make wudu now, slowly, noticing the water on hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet, then sit before you open the Qur'an. If that isn't yours, go and wash your hands and face, slowly, with full attention, and come back to sit before whatever you read next. Let the water be the beginning of the reading. The bell holds the time.
None touch it but the purified. A noble Qur'an in a guarded book, touched only by the purified, read by many as the angels, and honored on earth with wudu. Today's word.
screen: `NONE TOUCH IT BUT THE PURIFIED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: touched with purity. Today, before you open something that matters to you, a book, a letter, a message, wash your hands and take one breath first. Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: He is with you wherever you are
612.word: He is with you wherever you are
612.hook: He is with you wherever you are (57:4)
612.howItsDone: Some Muslims recall this verse when traveling or in unfamiliar places; the idea of ihsan, worshipping as though one sees God, is taught from the hadith of Jibril, where it follows islam and iman.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Al-Waqi'ah: none touch it but the purified, and your line was touched with purity. Did you wash before opening something that mattered? Today, Surah Al-Hadid, the Iron. Day six hundred twelve.

An airport gate at 5am. A hospital corridor. A new apartment with the boxes still taped shut. A hotel room in a city where you don't speak the language. Places like these can make a person feel strangely unhooked, as if they've left their whole life behind at the last address. Surah fifty-seven, Al-Hadid, has a short line for exactly that feeling. It sits in the middle of a verse about the heavens and the Throne, and it's only a few words long.

Surah Al-Hadid opens wide. Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God. Verse three gives four names in a row: he is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward. Then verse four. It describes God creating the heavens and the earth in six days, then establishing himself on the Throne. It says he knows what goes into the earth and what comes out of it, what comes down from the sky and what goes up into it. And then, in Pickthall: "and He is with you wheresoever ye may be." Wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Ma'akum: with you. Ayna ma kuntum: wherever you are. The verse ends: and God sees what you do. So how is God with you? Muslims have explained it in more than one way. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir said he is with you by his knowledge, his hearing and his sight, watching over you, while being above his Throne, as the same verse says. Others, among them Sufi writers, dwell on the nearness itself, and read it with another verse: God is nearer to a person than their jugular vein. Both readings agree on one thing: in the verse, there is no place out of his sight. The hadith of Jibril turns this into a way of worshipping. Asked what ihsan, excellence, is, the Prophet ﷺ said: to worship God as though you see him, and if you don't see him, he sees you. The airport gate, the hospital, the empty apartment: the verse doesn't make them less strange. It says you didn't arrive there alone.
screen: `THE FIRST, THE LAST, OUTWARD, INWARD.` · `WITH YOU, WHEREVER YOU ARE.` · `BY KNOWLEDGE AND SIGHT, OR NEARNESS.` · `IHSAN: AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it in the next new place. Before you get there, rehearse it now. Sit, and feel exactly where you are: the floor, the chair, the air on your skin. Breathe in: wherever. Breathe out: you are. Then picture the next unfamiliar place you'll walk into today or this week, a new room, a waiting area, a street. Imagine stepping in and saying the line quietly there. The bell holds the time.
He is with you wherever you are. Surah Al-Hadid, verse four: wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Today's word.
screen: `HE IS WITH YOU WHEREVER YOU ARE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wherever you are. Today, the next time you walk into a place you haven't been, say it under your breath at the door. Day six hundred twelve.

613.title: Hearts not yet soft?
613.hook: has the time not come for believers' hearts to humble themselves (57:16)
613.howItsDone: Muslim preachers and teachers often recite 57:16 as a call to renewed sincerity, and the story of Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's turning is widely told in sermons and books on repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, he is with you wherever you are, and your line was wherever you are. Did you say it at the door of a new place? Day six hundred thirteen.

There's a story told about a man named Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. In his youth, the story goes, he was a highway robber. One night he was climbing a wall to meet someone he shouldn't, and from a house nearby he heard a voice reciting the Qur'an. It was one verse, a question. He stopped on the wall and answered it out loud: yes, Lord, the time has come. He climbed down a different man, and the story remembers him afterward as an ascetic and a teacher. Today, that question.
screen: `A ROBBER ON A WALL AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Hadid, verse sixteen. Pickthall: "Is not the time ripe for the hearts of those who believe to submit to Allah's reminder and to the truth which is revealed". In Arabic it opens: alam ya'ni lilladhina amanu an takhsha'a qulubuhum. Notice who's being asked. Not unbelievers. Those who believe. The question is for people who already pray, already know the words. Has the time not come for their hearts to soften? The verb is takhsha'a, from khushu', the humble stillness that's meant to fill prayer. A heart with khushu' is a heart that has stopped resisting. Sahih Muslim preserves a striking line from the companion Ibn Mas'ud. He said that between the time they accepted Islam and the time God reproached them with this verse, there were only four years. Four years in, and already the question came: have you gotten used to it? The verse goes on to warn against hearts that grow hard as time stretches on. Then the very next verse offers the turn. Know, it says, that God brings the earth back to life after its death. A dead field after rain. Commentators read the two verses together: hardness isn't permanent, and a heart can be revived the way the ground is. Read that way, the Fudayl story, whatever its historical details, is the next verse acted out: a hard heart turned over in one night. And the verse's question has no date written on it. It stays open, for whoever hears it.
screen: `ASKED OF THOSE WHO BELIEVE.` · `KHUSHU': A HEART THAT STOPS RESISTING.` · `ONLY FOUR YEARS IN.` · `THE EARTH REVIVED AFTER ITS DEATH.`

segments.voice: The practice: let one hardness go. Sit, and breathe. Notice where you hold tension: jaw, shoulders, hands. Let them soften. Now think of one place your heart has gone hard: a grudge, a habit you've stopped noticing, a person you've stopped listening to. Don't fix it. Just hold it, and ask the verse's question quietly: has the time not come? On each out-breath, let a little of the hardness loosen. The bell holds the time.
Hearts not yet soft? Surah Al-Hadid asks believers whether the time has come for their hearts to humble themselves before God's reminder. Today's word.
Your line: has the time not come? Today, take one small step toward the thing you just held, a message, an apology, a single kind word. Day six hundred thirteen.

614.title: Play and amusement
614.hook: this life is play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth (57:20)
614.howItsDone: Muslim preachers often recite 57:20 in reminders about the passing nature of worldly life, while the hadith tradition also preserves room for play, sport and celebration, especially on the two Eids.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hearts not yet soft, and your line was has the time not come? Did you take your one small step? Day six hundred fourteen.

A toddler with a plastic bucket on the beach. A teenager scrolling at midnight. A thirty-year-old choosing the right outfit for a wedding. A forty-year-old mentioning, casually, the new car. A seventy-year-old counting grandchildren and property. Line them up and it looks like five different people wanting five different things. Surah Al-Hadid, verse twenty, lines up five words in a row. Some commentators have read them as exactly that: one life, seen from the beach to the end.

Pickthall: "Know that the life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and boasting among you, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children". In Arabic, the five are la'ib, play; lahw, amusement or diversion; zina, adornment; tafakhur, boasting to one another; and takathur, piling up more wealth and children than the next person. Some commentators noticed the order follows the stages of a life: the child plays, the youth is diverted, the young adult adorns, the grown person boasts, the old person counts what they've gathered. Then the verse gives a picture. It's like rain that brings up plants that delight the farmer. Then they dry, and you see them turn yellow, then they become straw. Green, yellow, straw. That's the life of the world, in one season. And then, in the next verse, a turn: race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord, and a garden as wide as the heavens and the earth. Is the verse against fun? The hadith collections suggest not. Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ let 'A'isha watch a group of Abyssinians performing with spears in the mosque on a feast day, standing so she could see over his shoulder until she'd had enough. The verse isn't banning the beach bucket. It's naming what play is: lovely, and passing, like grass after rain. The verse's warning is against mistaking it for the whole of life.
screen: `PLAY, AMUSEMENT, ADORNMENT.` · `BOASTING, AND PILING UP MORE.` · `GREEN, YELLOW, STRAW.` · `RACE TOWARD FORGIVENESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: put down one amusement for an hour. Sit, and breathe. Think of the thing that most often fills your spare minutes: a game, a feed, a show, a habit of checking. You don't need to judge it. Just picture setting it down for one hour today. Picture what might fill that hour instead: a walk, a person, a page, a prayer if you pray. Then let the picture rest, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Play and amusement. Surah Al-Hadid calls the life of the world play, amusement, adornment, boasting and rivalry, green, then yellow, then straw. Today's word.
Your line: play passes. Today, put your one amusement down for an hour, and notice what that hour turns into. Day six hundred fourteen.

615.title: Iron sent down
615.hook: We sent down iron with great strength and many uses (57:25)
615.howItsDone: Muslims read 57:25 as a summary of the messengers' mission: guidance, justice, and the strength to uphold it; the surah takes its name, Al-Hadid, from this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, play and amusement, and your line was play passes. What filled the hour you set aside? Today, the verse that gives Surah Al-Hadid its name. Day six hundred fifteen.

Look around the room you're in. The nails in the walls. The hinges on the door. The frame of the chair, the spring in the pen, the steel inside the concrete of the building. A kitchen knife, a hospital bed, a bridge, a sword. A great deal of modern life runs on iron, for building and for breaking. Surah fifty-seven is named Al-Hadid, the Iron, after one verse near its end. And that verse puts iron in a surprising company: right beside scripture and the scales of justice.

Verse twenty-five, in paraphrase. God sent his messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, so that people would stand up for justice. And God sent down iron, in which there is great strength and many benefits for people, and so that God may know who helps him and his messengers, unseen. Three things in one verse. The Book: guidance, what's right. The Balance: the mizan we met in Ar-Rahman, fairness, justice. And iron: power, the means to build, protect and defend. Commentators read it as a set. Guidance tells you what is just. The balance measures it. And iron is the strength that can either protect justice or crush it. The verb is the striking part: anzalna, we sent down. It's the same verb used for the Qur'an itself. What does it mean to send down iron? Classical commentators pointed to another verse, in Surah Az-Zumar, where God is said to have sent down cattle for people, eight kinds. There, sent down means created and provided as a gift from above. Some modern readers connect the verse to astronomy and the idea that iron came to the earth from beyond it. Others are cautious about reading science into a verse. Either way, the verse says something plain about strength: it's a trust. Iron has great power and many uses, and the same verse asks who will use it to help. The test isn't whether you have strength. It's what side of the balance you put it on.
screen: `THE BOOK, THE BALANCE, THE IRON.` · `STRENGTH TO PROTECT JUSTICE.` · `ANZALNA: WE SENT DOWN.` · `STRENGTH IS A TRUST.`

segments.voice: The practice: touch iron and think. Find something made of iron or steel near you: a key, a spoon, a door handle, a railing. Hold it. Feel its weight, its coolness, how it doesn't bend. Breathe. Now think of one strength you have: a skill, a position, a voice others listen to, physical strength. Ask the verse's question of it: what is this strength helping? Let the metal warm in your hand as you sit. The bell holds the time.
Iron sent down. Surah Al-Hadid places iron, with its great strength and many uses, beside the Book and the Balance. Today's word.
Your line: strength sent down. Today, use your one strength once on behalf of someone who has less of it. Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: Allah heard her
616.hook: Allah heard the woman who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and a ruling came (58:1)
616.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Khawla bint Tha'laba as an example of a woman whose plea was answered in the Qur'an; Islamic law treats zihar as forbidden and sets an expiation before a husband who said it may return to his wife.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Hadid with iron sent down, and your line was strength sent down. Who did your strength help? Today, a new surah, named for a woman. Day six hundred sixteen, the end of the week.

In a small room in Medina, a woman is speaking with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, low and urgent. Her husband, in anger, has said an old Arabian phrase to her: you are to me like my mother's back. By custom, that left a wife in limbo: not divorced, so she couldn't remarry, and not a wife, so he wouldn't come near her. She has children, and she's getting older. She argues her case. In the corner of the same house, the Prophet's wife 'A'isha can't even make out the words.

The woman is named in the reports as Khawla bint Tha'laba, and her husband as Aws ibn as-Samit. She pleaded, and she complained to God. And the surah that came down opens with her. Pickthall: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah." Qad sami'a Allah: God has heard. The surah is named for her: Al-Mujadila, she who disputes, she who pleads her case. A whole surah of the Qur'an, named for a woman who argued. The next verses settle the matter. Saying that phrase does not make a wife into a mother; it's a wrong and false thing to say. A man who says it and wants to return must make amends first: free a slave, or if he can't, fast two months in a row, or if he can't, feed sixty poor people. The old custom that trapped women was ended. And 'A'isha's reaction is the part people remember. The reports preserve her words: blessed is the One whose hearing takes in every voice. The woman was speaking to the Prophet in a corner of my house, and I couldn't hear what she said, and God heard her from above the seven heavens. Notice what the verse does not do. It doesn't scold her for arguing. It records her disputing and her complaint, and answers both. A voice too low for the next room was heard, and the answer became law for everyone after her.
screen: `KHAWLA PLEADS HER CASE.` · `QAD SAMI'A ALLAH: GOD HAS HEARD.` · `AN OLD CUSTOM ENDED.` · `HEARING THAT TAKES IN EVERY VOICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand up for yourself respectfully. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been quietly unhappy about but haven't said: at home, at work, with a friend. Picture Khawla, low-voiced and steady. Shape what you need into one calm, clear sentence, no blame, just the truth of it. If you pray, you might bring it to God first, as she did. Say the sentence silently a few times, until it feels steady. The bell holds the time.
Allah heard her. Surah Al-Mujadila opens: God has heard the woman who pleaded with the Prophet about her husband, and complained to God. Today's word.

Your line: she was heard. This week ran from the water you drink and the purified, through Al-Hadid's nearness, soft hearts, play and iron, to a woman who was heard. Today, say your calm sentence to the person it's for. Day six hundred sixteen.

original.note: Arabic: God has heard. The first words of Surah Al-Mujadila.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legal verse about marriage.
what it means: a woman's quiet plea, heard and answered, ending a custom that trapped wives.
what a scholar hears: zihar ('like my mother's back') ruled false in 58:2, with kaffara in 58:3–4; 'A'isha's words appear in Bukhari (Kitab at-Tawhid, ta'liq), an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.
